newsitem.title: PERU: Peru pressures rebels with armored car night moves.
newsitem.headline: Peru pressures rebels with armored car night moves.

text.p: Peru stepped up its pressure late on Friday to unnerve Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages by sending an armoured car at night to drive past the occupied Japanese ambassador's house on the 38th day of the siege.

Eight special forces police officers also went on foot up to the main entrance of the residence and trained their rifles on the building. Red laser beams were seen cutting across the garden to the building, witnesses said.

The night manoeuvres started at 10:30 p.m. (0330 GMT Saturday) and lasted about half an hour. The armoured vehicle approached the main entrance with special forces police on board aiming their rifles at the residence. But the vehicle stopped about 150 feet (50 metres) from the gate and reversed.

Accompanied by another group of at least six police -- creeping in single file pressed tight against the perimeter wall -- the armoured vehicle passed alongside two more sides of the compound before withdrawing from the area.
Earlier in the day, two personnel carriers passed by the siege site twice and a helicopter flew overhead with an armed policeman in a harness riding on its skids.

In response to the daylight manoeuvres, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels broadcast a revolutionary song for the second time and chants of "Long Live the Revolution" and "Long Live Freedom" could be heard from inside the residence. The rebels had broadcast the same song earlier as dawn broke.

The International Red Cross, which is carrying messages between the two sides and providing humanitarian relief to the hostages, temporarily suspended its activities at the siege site, saying it should have been informed of the police plans.
But after Red Cross representative Michel Minnig met with police officials the hostages received their daily ration of food and water only a few hours late.
While Minnig claimed all hostages were in "good" health, pressure was growing for a top judge to be released on medical grounds.
The Lima College of Lawyers published a message from key hostage Moises Pantoja, who lost his post as Supreme Court President while captive, written to his family from inside the residence.
"I can hardly walk. When I do, I lose my balance. My feet, hands and fingers have all gone hard. My arthritis stops me from reading and I can barely write," the message said.
Since seizing hundreds of guests when they stormed a party at the residence on Dec. 17, the rebels have freed most of their captives in what they called "goodwill gestures".
In the last three weeks, they have freed only one hostage, releasing on Jan. 17 a top police official for health reasons.

The armoured vehicles, each with a heavy machine gun on top, appeared at the siege site on Wednesday but Friday was the first day they crossed police cordons and lines of journalists two blocks from the residence to enter the restricted zone in front of the house.
They also crossed an area, marked out on Thursday by the Red Cross with white paint, which police were supposed to stay out of while the Red Cross was working at the residence.
The new police manoeuvres followed a warning by Fujimori on Thursday that he wanted to wipe out the MRTA after the crisis.
The roughly 15 rebels in the house are armed with assault rifles and grenade launchers and have mined and booby-trapped the compound against possible attack.

Though both sides have said they are willing to sit down to discuss a peaceful end to the crisis, Fujimori has ruled out starting talks until the rebels drop their demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
The rebels have said there is no point in talking unless that demand is on the agenda.
